bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds the jury verdict, Southwark Crown Court, and reported convictions involving four women, while intensifying condemnation through “cruelty,” “disgraced,” and the peripheral dog allegation.

summary: On Monday, Russell Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison at Southwark Crown Court. Judge Mr Justice Bennathan described the 51-year-old as a "sexual predator" for crimes against four women between 2004 and 2009.

Last week, a jury convicted Brand of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault following a four-week trial. He was cleared of two further rape charges and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.

Victim impact statements described feeling "powerless" due to Brand's influence, while Mr Justice Bennathan remarked he showed "a casual and arrogant disregard for a woman's right to say no." The judge added his entourage indulged his "dreadful behaviour."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham praised the victims' bravery, vowing to be "relentless in making whatever improvements we can" to support systems. The Metropolitan Police revealed Brand remains under investigation over two further rape allegations.

By the end of next year, the Prime Minister plans to establish rape and serious sexual offence teams in every police force. This initiative aims to provide victims the confidence to come forward with their allegations.
title: Source Icon

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Trump’s reversal as a “deranged” act by a “sore loser,” stressing “without proof” allegations and damage to electoral trust; center coverage more neutrally emphasizes his shift from accepting results while calling claims “baseless.” Right-leaning coverage instead foregrounds “unusual patterns,” voting machines, early-vote “dumps,” and an alleged Democratic “VOTE SHIFT,” using “exposing,” “legacy media,” and “huge step backwards” to portray possible wrongdoing and media neglect.

summary: Reversing his initial post-election stance where he indicated he would accept the outcome, President Trump took to Truth Social to question whether the midterm results were "honest," pointing to pre-election polling discrepancies and targeting voting machines.
In his online posts, Trump raised unsubstantiated claims regarding how votes were processed and tallied, echoing rhetoric from past election cycles.

The pivot back to questioning election integrity follows a decisive Democratic sweep that captured majorities in both the House and Senate, alongside several key gubernatorial and state-level victories.

Election officials, independent watchmakers, and bipartisan state authorities have repeatedly emphasized that there is no evidence of widespread fraud, system manipulation, or technical failures that altered the outcome of the midterms.
title: Trump questions midterm election integrity after previously accepting results

summary: President Donald Trump said a "great dislike" for Israel contributed to Republican midterm losses, claiming in a CBS 60 Minutes interview Sunday that his presence on the ballot would have changed the outcome.
Trump announced on election day he would end $4 billion in annual aid to Israel; Netanyahu later described the shift as a "partnership," though he did not confirm prior notice of the decision.
Even Vice President JD Vance suggested Republicans might rethink their support for Israel, while Trump argued protected nations must cover war costs, stating "Without us, Israel would not exist."

Israeli journalist Amir Tibon noted Democrats and Republicans are competing to distance themselves from Israel, while Israeli President Isaac Herzog tasked Gadi Eizenkot with forming the next government.
Herzog characterized the challenges facing the State of Israel as immense, emphasizing the nation must remain vigilant against ongoing schemes and threats from Iran.
title: Trump says ‘great dislike’ for Israel contributed to Republican midterm losses
DOJ Civil Division Head Is Latest to Resign After Midterms

summary: On Sunday, Nvidia 's board announced an independent investigation into whether CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, stating it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.

The inquiry follows reports that Huang maintained a relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom U.S. intelligence officials identified as a Chinese intelligence asset tasked with gathering information about advanced chips.

Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife in a memo to employees, taking "full responsibility" for his actions, while the board expressed confidence in his leadership and his commitment to cooperate fully with the investigation.

Republican lawmakers requested that Huang brief Congress regarding potential national security risks, while President Donald Trump called him "an honorable guy," and China's foreign ministry dismissed the allegations as "groundless smears and slander" on Monday.

Technology analyst Dan Ives called the probe "a black eye moment" for Huang, warning it could create an overhang on the stock, though he expects Huang to remain CEO while scrutiny over China chip sales intensifies.
title: Nvidia opens probe of CEO Huang being targeted by possible Chinese spy

summary: On Sunday, President Donald Trump said a return to war with Iran is "highly unlikely" if ongoing indirect negotiations produce progress, emphasizing diplomacy as his preferred path forward.

Diplomatic activity across the Middle East has intensified following the recent midterm elections. On Friday, Trump called Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani to discuss de-escalation, while Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi engaged regional counterparts.

Trump noted a third American aircraft carrier strike group recently arrived, declaring forces "fully locked and loaded." He assessed Iranian missile capacity at 10% and drone capabilities at 15% of normal levels.

The president identified 38 Iranian bridges and power plants as potential military targets, though he stated he prefers avoiding such destruction because rebuilding infrastructure would require 10 years.

Eight months into the stalemate, Iran faces 301% inflation amid frozen assets and oil sales restrictions. Trump repeated that new military action will most likely not be necessary if Tehran reaches a strong agreement.
title: Trump says he is unlikely to order Iran attack if talks progress, CNN reports

summary: The House will likely vote on impeaching Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth this week, with Republican leaders expecting the measure to pass with a simple majority despite party divisions.
Following Tuesday's midterm elections, lawmakers are pushing impeachment after the Iran war championed by Hegseth contributed to Republicans losing their congressional majority.
Rep. Thomas Massie is forcing the vote, and according to Axios, the political calculus "has now shifted dramatically" since Tuesday with GOP anger fueling impeachment support.
Chief spokesman Sean Parnell said Hegseth "will not back down," though removing him from office would require a two-thirds supermajority of 67 Senators in the Upper House.
While the current House may impeach, Democrats plan to make investigating the Department of War "a key focus of their agenda" next year, though removal remains unlikely in the Senate.
title: Jeffries Announces Support for Hegseth Impeachment

summary: On Saturday, President Donald Trump announced on Truth Social that he offered UFC CEO Dana White the position of White House Press Secretary.
The two men are longtime friends, with Trump hosting UFC Freedom 250 at the White House earlier this year and White speaking at Republican National Convention appearances.
Trump requested White bring mixed martial arts fighters, including Islam Makhachev and Kayla Harrison, as assistants to help "defend us against the Lunatic Left."
This announcement follows Trump replacing his White House chief of staff with Stephen Miller, as the administration reorganizes after Republicans lost both chambers of Congress on Tuesday.
While Trump claimed "Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other," it remains unclear whether the UFC executive intends to accept the offer.
title: Trump Says He Offered White House Press Secretary Job to UFC Chief Dana White

Right-Leaning coverage instead celebrates decisive leadership: “blunt post-election message,” “campaign is over,” and “move on” dismiss electoral maneuvering while foregrounding Hamas disarmament, demilitarization, and security obstacles.

summary: On Thursday, President Donald Trump phoned Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, urging him to implement the Gaza peace plan with verified disarmament and demilitarization of the Gaza Strip.

Implementation of the initiative stalled during Israel's October election, but the proposal calls for Hamas to surrender weapons and transfer governing authority to a new Palestinian technocratic administration.

The Board of Peace presented a $2.45 billion recovery initiative in September, outlining 66 projects for Gaza's postwar administration, though Netanyahu remains deeply skeptical that Hamas will disarm.

President Isaac Herzog tasked Gadi Eisenkot with forming a government on Sunday, giving him 28 days to assemble a majority as Eisenkot declared, "An absolute majority of Knesset members representing the Israeli public support change."
The Trump administration intends to advance the initiative regardless of who leads Israel, as Former British Prime Minister Tony Blair visited last week to urge leaders to support the proposal.
title: Trump Calls on Netanyahu in a Call to Implement the Gaza Peace Plan, According to Axios

summary: Following sweeping midterm victories, congressional Democrats are preparing aggressive investigations into the executive branch, prompting President Donald Trump and Attorney General Todd Blanche to signal a combative stance toward the incoming oversight drive.

On Saturday, Trump posted that Democrats were "going around threatening a lot of people," calling oversight plans "Weaponization and Lawfare at another level" and ordering the Justice Department to investigate.

Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries stated those "shortchanging the American people" must be held accountable, as lawmakers prepare to probe immunity deals, the pardon industry, and Jeffrey Epstein's investigative files.
Trump appointed longtime adviser Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff, while several prominent Justice Department officials recently departed following the midterm election results.

The administration's expansive view of executive power risks exacerbating conflicts between the Justice Department and Congress, potentially defining Trump's remaining two years in office as the oversight drive intensifies.
title: Trump and His Justice Department Stand Defiant as Democrats Ready an Investigative Blitz

bias: Left-Leaning coverage amplifies Biden’s sweeping indictment of Trump, using phrases such as “deeply damaged,” “tear down institutions,” “inflame hatreds,” and “to his grave” to frame January 6 as enduring moral culpability and part of a broader assault on democracy and social cohesion.

summary: The Atlantic published excerpts Monday from former President Joe Biden 's memoir, "Promise Me, America," containing his sweeping indictment of Donald Trump's 2020 election lies and Jan. 6 Capitol attack, which Biden says should "follow him to his grave."

Reflecting on his four years in office, Biden details efforts to restore global alliances and his decision to abandon his 2024 reelection bid. He writes that Trump's administration was determined to "tear down institutions and inflame hatreds."

Biden states that "Donald Trump led an insurrection" during the Jan. 6 Capitol attack and chided him for later issuing more than 1,500 pardons to offenders. He argues Trump's efforts to remain in power after losing the election represent a dangerous legacy.

In a social media post on Sunday, Biden announced he is undergoing prostate cancer treatment. He acknowledged he "won't be able to do as many conversations about my book as I'd hoped," though his doctors remain encouraged by his progress.

America is unique, Biden emphasized, because it was "built on an idea" that all people are created equal. He urged citizens to ensure the nation never forgets this principle, even as his full memoir releases Nov. 17.
title: Joe Biden, in White House Memoir, Says Trump Should Carry the Weight of Jan. 6 Riots 'to His Grave'

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds students’ “disruptions,” “challenging start,” and looming “financial pain,” framing closures as immediate social and economic harm.

Right-Leaning coverage emphasizes scale—1,156 schools closed, “highest since the pandemic”—alongside declining enrollment and reduced funding, while still acknowledging disruption but de-emphasizing individual experience.
The pivotal divide is whether closures are portrayed chiefly through personal consequences and future hardship or through statistics and fiscal pressures.

Across perspectives, closures, enrollment decline, and student adjustment remain shared concerns, reflecting competing social and demographic interpretations.
summary: Vallejo City Unified School District has closed five campuses since 2025, a quarter of its schools, addressing a reported $36 million deficit. The district now serves half as many students as it did two decades ago.

Nationwide, public school enrollment fell by more than 1.4 million students, roughly 3%, between fall 2019 and 2024, driven by lower birth rates and other factors. Researchers estimate schools could lose $11.5 billion in annual state revenue by 2030-2031.

Vallejo parent Kimberly Ninez-Brandão reported her daughter, Penny, faced a fifth-grade class with 32 students before the teacher resigned on a Tuesday in October. Such instability forces families to leave, further eroding per-student funding.

Research suggests closing schools rarely yields the financial relief districts hope for, as busing and severance costs consume potential savings. Studies from the University of Chicago indicate displaced students often suffer long-term drops in reading and math performance.

Lydia Rainey, research principal at the Center on Reinventing Public Education , warned the financial situation is unlikely to improve. With enrollment falling faster than closures, districts face more painful decisions ahead, including widespread layoffs and academic cuts.
title: U.S. School Closures Rise as Enrollment Falls and Districts Cut Costs

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the case through transparency and urgency, using terms such as “opposes,” “ban,” “assassinating,” and “pressure” to highlight media resistance to excluding cameras and calls from Kirk’s family, supporters, and President Trump for faster proceedings.

summary: Fourth District Judge Tony Graf is expected to establish a trial timeline today in Provo, Utah, for Tyler Robinson , who is accused of killing Charlie Kirk.

Robinson, 23, faces seven charges, including aggravated murder, for the September 10, 2025, shooting of Kirk at Utah Valley University; prosecutors allege Robinson targeted the Turning Point USA co-founder for political beliefs.

Defense attorney Staci Visser requested a provisional 2029 trial start, citing the need to review about 31,000 discovery documents and eight million digital artifacts; the team is about 25 per cent through the work.

The Utah County Attorney's Office proposed a 17-week trial beginning January 31, 2028, while Erika Kirk urged a 2027 start. President Donald Trump criticized Graf for "taking forever" to resolve the case.

Defense lawyers asked Graf to exclude electronic media from Monday's hearing, arguing broadcasting remarks could take them out of context; media organizations challenged the request, asserting the public deserves an unfiltered record.
title: A Utah judge is expected to set a trial date in Charlie Kirk’s killing

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds “unresolved global crises,” “questions” over the U.S. approach, and European demands for a “fair settlement,” portraying Rubio as being “pressed” to protect Kyiv and avoid Iran “escalation”; right-leaning coverage frames the same meeting as a test of U.S. leadership, stresses “no” Ukraine deal without Europe , urges Washington to “steer clear” of Iran, and highlights “real accountability” at the UN and an “innovation first agenda.” Center coverage emphasizes Trump’s “midterm setback” and uncertainty over multilateralism.
The pivotal divide is whether Paris represents scrutiny of U.S. policy or reinforcement of its priorities, though all stress Ukraine, Iran, allied influence, and wider security concerns.
summary: Foreign ministers from the G7 nations convened in Paris on Monday for two days of talks centered on the Russia-Ukraine war, Iran conflict, energy, and artificial intelligence.

This gathering follows massive midterm election losses for President Donald Trump's Republican Party, prompting allies to question whether the administration will alter its foreign policy approach regarding Ukraine and the Middle East.

The meeting coincides with U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday, where European leaders fear Kyiv could face pressure to accept disadvantageous terms for ending the war.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told RTL radio that "Europeans will be represented and France will participate in these talks," addressing concerns about exclusion from U.S.-led diplomatic processes.

Beyond Ukraine, diplomats aim to address rising Iran tensions and energy stability, while United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio faces questions regarding U.S. sanctions against the International Criminal Court.
title: G7 allies to assess impact of Trump's midterm setback at Paris talks

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the Republican-controlled session as a “crammed” opportunity to finish a “lengthy to-do list,” stressing unfinished work and “little bipartisan appetite.” Right-leaning coverage emphasizes Republicans’ remaining authority and urgency before Democrats take power, using more dramatic language such as “midterm upheaval,” “brutal,” and a profane “closet” metaphor.
Center coverage foregrounds the December 11 funding deadline, shutdown risk, and a potential “power struggle,” while de-emphasizing partisan blame.
The sharpest divide is whether the session represents Republican responsibility, residual leverage, or institutional crisis.
All perspectives emphasize the short calendar, backlog, party transition, funding, and farm-bill challenges, reflecting broader disputes over governance and power.
summary: On December 11, federal funding expires, forcing the Republican-led Congress to navigate a final legislative window before Democrats assume control of both chambers on January 3, 2027.

Lawmakers return to Washington on Monday for a lame-duck session, the period between the November election and January 3, 2027, when outgoing members attempt to finalize unfinished legislative business.
Congress must address the National Defense Authorization Act and the overdue Farm Bill, which lawmakers have struggled to pass amid long-running partisan disagreements over spending priorities.

Without new funding legislation, federal agencies face a potential shutdown beginning December 12, forcing lawmakers to choose between full-year spending bills, a short-term extension, or a funding lapse.

Analysts suggest Democrats may prefer postponing major spending decisions until next year, when they hold power, complicating Republican efforts to resolve budget negotiations before losing control of Congress.
title: Congress faces crammed lame-duck session with little bipartisan appetite

summary: On Wednesday, federal agents detained an 8-year-old Haitian boy during a scheduled immigration check-in in San Diego, removing the Fay Elementary School student from his uncle's care after he lost Temporary Protected Status earlier this year.

The boy had lived with his uncle in City Heights since his father's deportation nearly two years ago. ICE claimed the uncle could not establish legal guardianship, leading agents to treat the child as an unaccompanied minor under the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act.

San Diego Unified School District Board Trustee Cody Petterson and City Councilmember Sean Elo-Rivera are demanding the child's release. Elo-Rivera called the detention "incredibly cruel," emphasizing the need for educational continuity for the 3rd grader.

Federal authorities transferred the child to the Office of Refugee Resettlement, though local officials remain unsure of his exact whereabouts. Advocates, including the Haitian Bridge Alliance, continue pressuring the administration for his return to family.

The case illustrates broader concerns regarding the revocation of Temporary Protected Status and its impact on students. Rep. Juan Vargas and other leaders are calling on the Trump Administration to restore the program and prioritize keeping children with established support systems.
title: 8-Year-Old Haitian Boy Placed in Federal Custody Alone After ICE Check-in, Advocates Say

summary: United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated there is "no progress to report" in efforts to end the West Asia war, describing Iranian demands as "outrageous" and "ridiculous."
Tehran has demanded an end to naval blockades and sanctions as conditions for peace talks, while Washington seeks concessions on Iranian nuclear programmes and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

Rubio said Washington would defend American forces and shipping if threatened; President Donald Trump told CNN it is "highly unlikely" he would order further strikes if Tehran agrees to a strong agreement.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told the Islamic Republic News Agency there has been "no activity or movement" from mediators following United States midterm elections.
Qatar continues mediating between Washington and Tehran as diplomatic efforts face hurdles, with Trump scheduled to meet Qatar's leader to discuss stalled negotiations.
title: Iran defends two-day proposal for peace talks after US rejects conditions

summary: On Sunday, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani sat down with Fox News host Shannon Bream to discuss his socialist views and Democratic Socialists of America platform, surprising Bream with his specific policy positions.

Following high-profile midterm wins for progressive candidates last week, Bream asked Mamdani to address critics of the left's growing influence on the Democratic Party and which specific goals mainstream America might embrace.

When Bream pressed on specific DSA platform items, Mamdani rejected abolishing the Senate, Supreme Court, prisons, and borders, though he identified 'abolishing ICE' as the platform item most 'acceptable' to mainstream America.

Responding to Bream's questioning about internal party divisions, Mamdani said DSA members are united by a belief in the 'dignity of working-class people' and meaningful democratic work beyond the ballot box.

For the 2028 election cycle, the New York City Mayor is reportedly positioning himself as a 'progressive kingmaker' to mobilize the left, as he is constitutionally ineligible to serve as president himself.
title: Mamdani: Abolishing ICE is the most ‘acceptable’ part of DSA platform to ‘mainstream America’

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds privacy and immigrant vulnerability, stressing that the city “must” disclose shelter residents’ names and portraying the ICE request as “political” rather than investigatory; right-leaning coverage frames the same ruling as a legal defeat for Mamdani, using “overrode,” “win,” “enforcement,” and “sanctuary objections” to celebrate compelled compliance, while emphasizing claims that records were limited to people linked to serious or violent crimes.
Center coverage stays institutionally focused on Judge Kaplan’s order.

summary: On Friday, United States District Judge Lewis Kaplan ordered New York City to provide Immigration and Customs Enforcement with names and birth dates of specific Bronx shelter residents despite the city's repeated attempts to block the subpoena.

City Hall had fought the subpoena, arguing the request was 'more political than investigatory' and an attempt to 'circumvent and undermine' sanctuary laws protecting more than 2,000 migrants at the South Bronx facility.

While ICE originally sought broad access, the ruling directs appointment of a special master to identify only residents with 'certain serious criminal histories,' and Judge Lewis Kaplan gave the city two weeks to devise a compliance plan.

The New York Immigration Coalition is urging Mayor Zohran Mamdani to appeal the order, arguing that compliance violates local laws limiting cooperation between city agencies and federal immigration enforcement.

This ruling tests New York City's sanctuary protections, established in 2014 to limit federal cooperation, while facing ongoing litigation from the Trump administration aimed at dismantling these local policies.
title: Federal Judge Rules NYC Must Give ICE Names of Bronx Shelter Residents
B.C. Lab Ordered to Pay $32K for Misgendering Transgender, Non-Binary Patients

summary: On Monday, the Supreme Court declined to hear a dispute between Roberto Clemente's sons and Puerto Rico over commemorative license plates, leaving lower court rulings intact without explanation.

Puerto Rico issued the plates in 2022 for the 50th anniversary of the Pittsburgh Pirates legend's death, charging $21 and $5 fees that raised $15 million for the territory rather than the Clementes' businesses.

The Clementes asked the Supreme Court to find that Puerto Rico violated the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution, but lower courts previously dismissed the case by finding the territory immune from such lawsuits.
Lawyers for Puerto Rico Gov. Pedro Pierluisi-Urrutia argued the issues were not worth hearing, writing, "Neither question warrants this Court's review," citing established precedent.
Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts, who pledged to "call balls and strikes" in legal disputes, presided over the court's refusal to intervene, leaving territorial immunity rulings standing.
title: US Supreme Court rejects dispute over Roberto Clemente license plates in Puerto Rico

summary: Nvidia shares fell approximately 7% on Monday following reports about CEO Jensen Huang's personal life and a possible foreign intelligence investigation.
The company is investigating reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
The decline comes amid growing concerns about the sustainability of AI investments and data center expansion, causing technology stocks to fall.
Nvidia shares are down more than 20% from their peak, while the Nasdaq entered correction territory after dropping over 10% from its recent high.
title: Nvidia shares slide as US tech giant investigates CEO's affair with suspected Chinese spy

summary: On Sunday, the Financial Times reported that Anthropic struck a deal worth about $3.4 billion to secure 1.7 gigawatts of gas-fired generators for data centers .
San Antonio, Texas-based OnePWR Solutions had ordered the generators from Caterpillar two years ago but needed money to complete the purchase.
Rather than acquiring the supplier, Anthropic took over existing orders and installation responsibilities, keeping OnePWR independent while securing engineering capabilities needed for deployment.
As the company prepares for its IPO, this purchase supports infrastructure expansion following last week's amended filing that revealed $895bn in total commitments.
The startup expects to spend more than $500 billion over 10 years on infrastructure, reflecting an industry trend where Elon Musk's firm faces litigation in Memphis over similar gas turbines.
title: Anthropic Secures $3.4 Billion Generator Deal for AI Data Centers, FT Reports

summary: On Friday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended President Donald Trump's decision to launch the war against Iran at the Conservative Political Action Conference, arguing it was necessary to safeguard the world from Iranian nuclear ambitions.
Republicans lost both chambers of Congress in Tuesday's elections, with voters blaming Trump's policies for economic strain, including higher energy prices from disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

The International Atomic Energy Agency reports Iran holds 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60% purity, while the U.S. military continues limited strikes, including disabling a commercial ship Saturday that allegedly breached a naval blockade.

Conservative commentators and voters condemned Rubio's defense; one user describing herself as a "TradCatholic" wrote that Trump "burned down the conservative Repub party by showing who he really is."

title: Trump’s war against Iran not ‘necessarily popular’ but needed to stop a nuclear threat, Rubio says

summary: On Tuesday, President Donald Trump announced plans to end approximately $4 billion in annual United States military aid to Israel by the end of 2026, citing an earlier agreement with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed welcomed the decision during an appearance on Thursday's Morning Joe, stating, "I think the president is actually right on this policy."

El-Sayed, the first Muslim American elected to the Senate, called for halting American arms sales to Israel, arguing taxpayer dollars should not fund actions he described as "genocide" and "apartheid" in Gaza and the West Bank.

The Democrat rejected claims that criticizing Israel constitutes antisemitism, emphasizing the need to separate Judaism from Israeli government policies while affirming commitment to Jewish children's safety.
El-Sayed advocated for a broader review of military support for Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Pakistan, arguing American taxpayer dollars should be prioritized for domestic needs instead.
title: El-Sayed backs Trump plan to end Israel aid: ‘I agree with him on that’

summary: On Monday, the Crown withdrew all criminal charges against 44 pro-Palestinian protesters arrested during an April 2024 sit-in at a downtown Montreal Scotiabank, officially ending the prosecution.
Protesters occupied the branch demanding Scotiabank divest from Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems, a move the bank eventually completed, which activists welcomed as a victory.

While 14 individuals previously pleaded guilty to municipal noise bylaw violations and paid $300 fines, defense lawyer Barbara Bedont noted most other protesters resolved their cases through community service.
Defendants challenged the charges under the Charter, arguing police violated their rights, and filed a formal complaint against the presiding judge alleging bias and unfair treatment.
Defense counsel Bedont warned that criminalizing peaceful sit-ins threatens the right to protest, suggesting the group's legal strategy likely influenced the Crown's decision to drop charges.
title: No Criminal Charges for Montreal Protesters Arrested at Bank Sit-In

summary: On Monday, Honda Motor announced a $3 billion investment to build a new assembly plant in Marysville, Ohio, expected to begin production in 2029 with an annual capacity for 240,000 vehicles and create more than 2,000 jobs.

American Honda Motor executive Jennifer Thomas cited the need to 'maximize the existing capacity' as automakers increasingly build in the United States to navigate President Donald Trump's tariffs and rising logistics costs.

Since beginning production in 1982, Honda has built more than 33 million vehicles and 39 million engines across 12 United States manufacturing plants. Nearly all vehicles sold in the U.S., including Acura models, are North American-produced, with more than 60% built domestically.

Volkswagen-Owned Audi announced it would invest more than $4 billion in a Georgia facility roughly two weeks before Honda's announcement. General Motors, Ford Motor, Toyota Motor, and Hyundai Motor also recently committed billions to U.S. operations.

Thomas warned the industry faces a 'catastrophic' scenario if the U.S. and Canada fail to reach a trade deal by year-end. Trump has threatened to increase tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts from 25% to 50% on Jan. 1 if negotiations stall.
title: Honda to invest $3 billion in new vehicle assembly plant in Ohio

summary: On Sunday, Democratic House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries ruled out working with incoming White House chief of staff Stephen Miller , declaring that cooperation with him is "not going to happen."
President Donald Trump announced Friday that Miller would replace Susie Wiles as chief of staff, elevating the architect of the administration's aggressive immigration agenda to the top staff role.

During an appearance on ABC's "This Week," Jeffries denounced Miller as a "dangerous xenophobe," accusing him of directing a "violent mass deportation machine" that brutalized American citizens including Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good.

Following midterm victories, Democrats vowed to maintain a "firewall" in Congress against the administration, with Jeffries arguing that voters rejected "that kind of MAGA extremism" across House, Senate, and state races.

Despite the sharp rejection of Miller, Jeffries signaled that Democrats remain open to negotiating with Trump on other legislative priorities, noting Trump's stated openness to deals in a 60 Minutes interview scheduled for Sunday night.
title: Jeffries Says Democrats Won’t Work With Incoming Chief of Staff Stephen Miller

summary: On Friday, two Newport Beach fishermen rescued a Royal Caribbean employee treading water 20 miles off the Southern California coast, identifying him as a pianist aboard the Ovation of the Seas.
Newport Beach Lifeguard Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda estimated the man fell overboard around 2:30 a.m., roughly nine hours before rescue, while the U.S. Coast Guard investigates the incident.
Fishermen Sean Norton and Grant Garrett spotted the man near Catalina Island while returning from a fishing trip, with Norton recalling, "Grant and I each got an arm and lifted him up."

Responding lifeguards transported the man to a hospital where he is expected to survive, and Royal Caribbean stated, "We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time."

Norton credited survival to 76-degree water during a strong El Niño year, stating, "A different year, no way he makes it," though passengers reported no emergency alerts before disembarking and the Coast Guard investigation remains ongoing.
title: Pianist who fell from cruise ship found alive by Californian fishermen nine hours later

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames El Niño as “colliding” with human-caused warming, portraying a “new age of climate extremes” and urging leaders to “get serious”; it elevates Berkeley Earth’s 95% chance that 2026 breaks the record and links COP31 to climate finance and political action.
Right-Leaning coverage foregrounds El Niño “supercharging” weather, historical rankings, nine datasets, and hazards such as fires and floods, while de-emphasizing those political demands.
Center coverage emphasizes the estimated 0.1–0.2°C boost and possibility of a warmer 2027.
All acknowledge WMO’s 1.47°C rise and unusually warm years, reflecting shared concern filtered through ideological disputes over causation and policy.
summary: On Monday, the World Meteorological Organisation warned that a Super El Niño is 'off the charts,' with global temperatures reaching about 1.47°C above pre-industrial averages as the phenomenon 'supercharges' weather patterns.
El Niño is a recurring climate phenomenon across the tropical Pacific that shifts irregularly every two to seven years, triggering predictable disruptions of temperature, winds, and precipitation.

Extreme weather has already caused devastating impacts: more than 30,000 excess deaths in Europe , 1,300 deaths from Himalayan flash floods in Nepal, and 146.5 million people in India exposed to extreme heat.
The El Niño Heat Mortality Tracker reveals an extra 370,000 lives could be at risk over the next six months, with Nigeria, India, and Brazil forecast to bear the brunt of the crisis.
Countries are gathering in Turkey from November 9 to 20 for climate talks, where the WMO State of the Climate report will provide essential data to inform international discussions.
title: This year set to be one of four hottest on record, UN report says

summary: On Sunday, Former President Joe Biden announced he will limit promotional appearances for his memoir, Promise Me, America, citing ongoing prostate cancer treatment that has slowed him down.
Biden's office disclosed in May 2025 that he was diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer that had spread to his bones, requiring radiation treatments since then.
Releasing November 17, the memoir covers Biden's four years in office, including the COVID-19 pandemic, the January 6 Capitol riot, and his decision to end his 2024 re-election bid.
Acknowledging the disease's physical toll, the 83-year-old Democrat noted, "Some days are better than others," while his doctors remain "encouraged" by his treatment response.
Since leaving office in January 2025, Biden has maintained a low-profile life amid criticism regarding his mental fitness and his role in Donald Trump's 2024 election victory.
title: Joe Biden to scale back book tour as cancer ‘slows me down’

summary: On Sunday, November 8, 2026, President Donald Trump told CBS' 60 Minutes that his mass deportation policy was "too tough," acknowledging it may have contributed to Republican losses in last Tuesday's midterm elections.

Republicans suffered heavy losses in the midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, as officials attributed the defeat primarily to voter dissatisfaction with economic policies and the war with Iran.
Despite Trump's softer tone, Immigration and Customs Enforcement remains under strict orders to lock in roughly 19,000 arrests weekly, or about 2,700 people daily, officials told CBS News.
Signaling no policy slowdown, President Trump appointed immigration hawk Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff on Friday, November 6, 2026, days before the interview aired.

Starting January 3, 2027, Democrats will control Congress, armed with subpoena power and committee gavels to investigate enforcement practices and potentially limit funding for the mass deportation mandate.
title: Trump says immigration crackdown was 'too tough' and played part in midterms defeat

Center coverage bridges both, emphasizing the “trade war,” the January endpoint, negotiations, and suspended port fees.

summary: On Monday, China extended the suspension of its 24% tariff on United States imports for two months starting Tuesday, though a 10% tariff remains in effect.

Beijing stated the extension implements the "outcomes and consensus reached at the Washington meeting between the heads of state of China and the United States," following a proposed $60 billion reciprocal tariff cut package.
China also extended the pause on special port fees for US-linked vessels until Jan 10, 2027, and kept a probe into shipping and shipbuilding supply chains on hold.

Beijing noted the United States intends to use Section 301 tariffs to replace those imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act that courts held invalid, and will "closely follow subsequent measures taken by the US side."

President Donald Trump expects to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the APEC leaders' summit in Shenzhen next week to discuss denuclearisation and "trying to end the war in Iran.
title: China extends suspensions of 24% tariff on US goods, port fees on US ships for two months
